# HyperFund / HyperVerse: Investigation of the Alleged Crypto Fraud Network

## Executive assessment

Based solely on the supplied evidence, HyperFund appears to have operated as a crypto-related investment and recruitment network that combined four mutually reinforcing features: promised passive returns, multi-level recruitment incentives, credibility-building public promotion, and repeated rebranding. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) alleges that the structure functioned as both a Ponzi scheme—using new investor funds to support withdrawals or rewards—and a pyramid scheme—using recruitment incentives to attract additional participants. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) separately brought criminal charges against Sam Lee and Rodney Burton and reported Brenda Chunga’s guilty plea in January 2024. These remain allegations as to Lee and Burton unless and until established in court; Chunga’s guilty plea is a judicially significant admission of criminal responsibility for the charged conspiracy. ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S2](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The evidence supports a concrete conclusion: the network’s recruitment strategy was not based primarily on demonstrable commercial revenue. Instead, it appears to have relied on exceptionally high promised returns, referral-based expansion, claims of large-scale cryptocurrency mining, prominent personalities, and successive identity changes that helped preserve investor interest after operational problems emerged. The alleged use of a questionable “Steven Reece Lewis” CEO persona was particularly important because it supplied a new corporate face during the transition from HyperFund to HyperVerse, while the SEC alleges that the person was actually a paid actor portraying a fabricated character. ([S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

## Scope and source assessment

Four source records were supplied:

| Source ID | Source | Evidentiary significance |
|---|---|---|
| [S1] | CNBC, January 29, 2024 | Contemporary news account summarizing DOJ and SEC actions |
| [S2] | U.S. Department of Justice case page | Official case status, charges, allegations, and later procedural update |
| [S3] | The Guardian, January 3, 2024 | Investigative reporting concerning the alleged CEO persona and promotional operation |
| [S4] | SEC complaint filed January 29, 2024 | Primary civil pleading containing detailed allegations, amounts, mechanisms, and named relationships |

[S4] and [S2] are the strongest sources for legal allegations and procedural status because they are official government records. [S3] is valuable for independent reporting about the identity and credentials of “Steven Reece Lewis.” [S1] provides a concise contemporaneous account but is less detailed than the SEC complaint. The report distinguishes allegations from established procedural facts.

## Network identity and evolution

The project was presented under several related names. The SEC complaint states that the HyperTech Group launched HyperFund in June 2020, that it was rebranded as HyperVerse around December 2021, and that it was rebranded again as HyperNation around May 2022. The DOJ identifies the same associated names, including HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. ([S2](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The rebranding was not merely cosmetic in the allegations. HyperFund initially emphasized decentralized finance and crypto investment. HyperVerse shifted the narrative toward a virtual world or metaverse, including a new native token called HVT. HyperNation then used language about decentralized government, inequality, injustice, and blockchain-enabled autonomy. The SEC alleges that these changes were successive versions of the same underlying project rather than independent businesses. ([S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

This sequence appears to have served two related functions. First, it allowed the promoters to associate the project with changing technology trends: decentralized finance, metaverse applications, and blockchain-based governance. Second, it gave the network a means of presenting operational difficulties as a transition to a new platform rather than as evidence of a failed investment program. The SEC alleges that the transition from HyperFund to HyperVerse was largely automatic for investors, although the original website was disabled and investors were directed to the new site. ([S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

## Alleged Ponzi and pyramid mechanics

### Promised passive returns

The central financial proposition was the sale of “memberships.” According to the SEC complaint, investors could purchase packages at levels including $300, $500, $1,000, and $10,000, generally using Tether (USDT). Their membership value was represented internally through “HyperUnits,” with a $300 membership reflected as 300 HyperUnits. ([S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

Promotional materials allegedly promised daily passive rewards of between 0.5% and 1% until the investor’s original investment was doubled or tripled. The SEC complaint states that the project represented that an investor could triple the initial investment within 600 days. Chunga reportedly told prospective investors that they could recover their initial membership in approximately seven months and thereafter treat subsequent returns as “pure profit.” ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

These returns were economically extraordinary. A daily return of 0.5% implies simple annualized returns of approximately 182.5%, before compounding; a 1% daily return implies approximately 365% on a simple annual basis. The promotional structure therefore created a powerful recruitment message: investors were allegedly told they could earn substantial returns without conventional work or business activity. This calculation is an assessment based on the stated daily rates, not a claim that the scheme actually paid those rates consistently.

### Recruitment and downline incentives

The alleged scheme also contained a classic recruitment component. Investors could earn “accelerated” or leveraged rewards by recruiting others. The SEC describes Community Rewards, VIP Rewards, and Global Rewards. Community Rewards allegedly paid 20% of the membership value of a recruiter’s downline across as many as 20 levels. VIP rewards provided additional daily payments when a participant generated specified amounts of membership sales. Global Rewards allegedly pooled 4% of company sales for distribution among top promoters. ([S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

This structure is the basis for describing the project as pyramid-like. The earning opportunity was not limited to returns from an underlying productive asset; it also depended on expanding the participant network. The SEC alleges that Chunga reached the highest promoter level, “VIP 5 STAR,” within approximately six months, a status that required at least $5 million in referred investments or “sales.” ([S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

### Alleged absence of genuine mining revenue

The principal explanation offered to investors for the promised rewards was alleged large-scale crypto mining. Promotional presentations reportedly described warehouses operating around the world and mining Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies. The DOJ states that investors were falsely told their returns would be paid from mining operations that did not exist. ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S2](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

The SEC complaint alleges that Lee later admitted the HyperTech Group had exited Bitcoin mining in 2019, before HyperFund was launched, because mining was not profitable. The complaint further alleges that Lee acknowledged that promotional narratives about being a major miner were inaccurate but allowed those representations to continue. ([S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

On the evidence supplied, the mining narrative appears to have performed an explanatory and legitimizing role. It provided a purported source of revenue for the fixed rewards while also giving the project a technologically sophisticated identity. The SEC alleges, however, that HyperFund had no meaningful revenue source apart from investor funds and that withdrawals were paid with new deposits. That is the core Ponzi allegation. ([S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

## Public promoters and credibility construction

### Brenda Chunga

Brenda Chunga, also known as “Bitcoin Beautee,” was allegedly one of the network’s most prominent U.S. promoters. The SEC alleges that she hosted Zoom presentations, used promotional slide decks, recruited investors, and directly accepted money from some investors. The complaint alleges that Chunga received approximately $2.5 million in withdrawals from the platform and an additional $1.1 million from investors, for approximately $3.7 million in total. ([S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The complaint further alleges that Chunga used proceeds for luxury expenditures, including a birthday event that doubled as a recruitment event, jewelry, clothing, a BMW, designer handbags, a $1.2 million Maryland home, and a $1.1 million Dubai condominium. These allegations matter to the recruitment model because visible wealth could function as testimonial evidence to potential investors: the promoter appeared to embody the promised financial success. ([S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The DOJ reports that Chunga pleaded guilty in January 2024 to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud. The DOJ page identifies her case as United States v. Brenda Chunga, docket number 24-CR-1. ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S2](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

### Sam Lee and institutional credibility

Sam Lee, also identified as Xue Samuel Lee, was described by the DOJ and SEC as a co-founder or central figure. Promotional materials allegedly used Lee’s background, public appearances, and association with Blockchain Global to create credibility. The SEC alleges that he was involved throughout the project’s lifecycle, including during the HyperVerse launch and after the collapse, when he appeared in videos concerning possible recovery plans. ([S2](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The SEC also alleges that promotional materials falsely or misleadingly associated HyperFund with DigitalX and IBM, and emphasized Blockchain Global despite the company’s deteriorating condition. DigitalX allegedly issued a February 2021 notice disclaiming any affiliation with HyperTech Group, HyperFund, or related projects. ([S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

## The questionable “Steven Reece Lewis” CEO persona

The HyperVerse launch introduced “Steven Reece Lewis” as CEO in December 2021. Promotional materials attributed to him included degrees from the University of Leeds and the University of Cambridge, work at Goldman Sachs, the sale of a web-development company to Adobe, and the launch of an information-technology startup. The Guardian reported that it could not verify these credentials: the universities reportedly had no records, Companies House and SEC records did not show a matching person or company, Adobe filings did not show the claimed acquisition, and Goldman Sachs reportedly found no employment record. ([S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

The SEC goes further, alleging that the person presented as Lewis was a paid actor portraying a fabricated character and was not the actual CEO. The SEC complaint states that the actor worked as a television presenter in Bangkok and that Lee knew or was reckless in not knowing that the supposed CEO was not genuine. ([S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

Celebrity video endorsements reportedly accompanied the launch, including messages from Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass. The Guardian reported that the messages could have been obtained through Cameo-style paid celebrity video services, although it found no suggestion that those celebrities understood the alleged investment model. ([S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

The CEO persona therefore appears, on the supplied evidence, to have been a credibility device rather than an independently verifiable corporate executive. This is a significant assessment, not an independent finding beyond the SEC’s allegation and the Guardian’s reporting.

## Collapse and investor-withdrawal problems

Withdrawal problems emerged during the transition period. The SEC alleges that investors experienced difficulty withdrawing in November or December 2021 and generally could not withdraw by February or March 2022. It further alleges that the HOO Exchange suspended withdrawals in June 2022 and had stopped functioning by November 2022, preventing investors from redeeming their investments. ([S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The DOJ describes the alleged scheme as operating from June 2020 through November 2022 and states that withdrawals began to be blocked at least by July 2021. CNBC reports the same DOJ allegation. The dates are not fully consistent across the supplied materials, but all sources agree that withdrawals were restricted before the network’s effective collapse in 2022. ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S2](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

## Scale, legal posture, and contradictions

The reported scale varies. CNBC describes a $1.9 billion scheme, while the DOJ page refers to $1.89 billion. The SEC complaint states that more than $1.7 billion was raised worldwide. The Guardian cites a Chainalysis estimate of $1.3 billion in consumer losses during 2022. These figures may measure different things—total funds raised, alleged fraud amount, or estimated consumer losses—but the supplied sources do not fully reconcile them. ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S2](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist); [S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

As of the supplied DOJ page updated July 29, 2026, Rodney Burton had been sentenced to 32 months’ imprisonment, with credit for time served since January 3, 2024, followed by three years of supervised release. The same page says Chunga’s sentencing was continued to January 7, 2027. Lee’s criminal case remained identified by docket number 24-CR-21 in the supplied record, but the record does not state a final disposition for him. ([S2](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

## Conclusion

The evidence presents HyperFund/HyperVerse as an alleged fraud network whose effectiveness depended on combining financial promises with social proof. The passive-reward model attracted capital; the referral system converted participants into recruiters; public promoters displayed apparent success; the mining narrative supplied a purported economic explanation; rebranding preserved the project’s relevance; and the questionable CEO persona supplied a new executive identity during the HyperVerse phase. In my assessment, these were not isolated promotional features. They formed an integrated recruitment architecture in which credibility claims compensated for the absence of verifiable operating evidence, while rebranding and delayed withdrawals prolonged participation after the original investment proposition had become unstable.

The strongest evidence for this assessment is the convergence between the SEC’s detailed complaint, the DOJ’s criminal case summary, and the Guardian’s independent investigation. Nevertheless, the allegations against Lee and other unconvicted participants must remain legally characterized as allegations. The supplied record establishes a serious and extensively documented enforcement case, but it does not by itself establish every factual allegation beyond the legal proceedings described.
